newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bank of France spat throws spotlight on Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Bank of France spat throws spotlight on Chirac.

text.p: No sooner does President Jacques Chirac re-establish his credentials as a defender of franc stability and the drive to European monetary union, than a new row breaks out which leaves everyone asking questions again.

This time the question is whether Chirac will use the expiry of the mandates of two members of the independent Bank of France's monetary policy council to appoint candidates who will tip the balance in favour of faster monetary easing.

It is one that raises issues at the heart of a debate here on Europe -- like the decade-old commitment to the franc-mark link, seen as the precursor of the euro, or French uneasiness about giving too much power to an independent central bank.
It could even be a dress rehearsal for a bigger power struggle over the role of the future European Central Bank.
Two members of the Bank's nine-member policy council, former journalist Jean Boissonnat and ex-banker Bruno de Maulde, see their mandates expire in January.

Both are believed to be part of a six-man majority backing governor Jean-Claude Trichet's policies of giving priority to the stability of the franc-mark exchange rate, even if that means being ultra-cautious about lowering interest rates.

Lined up against that orthodoxy are at least two council members -- Paul Marchelli and Jean-Pierre Gerard -- who have spoken out in favour of faster rate cuts to boost growth. A third, Denise Flouzat, is believed to support them.

Sources familiar with the debate say Marchelli and Gerard would like to get French rates below German rates. Trichet, mindful of a 1993 attempt to do the same thing that ended in a franc crisis, will not countenance this.

So Chirac, who sparred with Trichet in his 1995 presidential election campaign, now has a chance to reduce or wipe out the governor's majority and to produce a council more willing to cut rates to help revive economic growth.

The danger is that such a council might be more cavalier on the franc-mark link and jeopardise the Franco-German partnership, seen as essential to the successful launch of Europe's single currency in January 1999.
Chirac, in a television interview last Thursday, again ruled out a franc devaluation as "unacceptable for the Germans".
"Interest rates are already very low. And Chirac has said he favours franc stability," Daiwa Research Institute economist Bernard Godement said.
Six candidates have been proposed to replace the two, given a three-year term when the monetary policy council first met on January 7, 1994, after the central bank became independent.
Boissonat is one of these six, while two others, Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard, are reported by newspapers to favour faster rates cuts. Both are close to Chirac.

One source familiar with the nomination process said he believed Chirac had intervened to get Guillen and Bernard on the list, put forward by the heads of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the head of the Economic and Social Council (CES). Chirac's office has declined all comment.
The next step is for the monetary policy council to give its own, unpublished, opinion on the list, and then for the cabinet to name the two Bank of France members.

Although the law making the Bank of France independent requires new members to be named at least eight days before the expiry of the mandates of outgoing members, the government looks set to break this in practice. The next cabinet meeting is not scheduled until January 2 or 3.

One possible compromise would be to name either Guillen or Bernard, whittling down Trichet's majority, while also appointing a more orthodox candidate -- Boissonnat or someone of similar views. Trichet's own mandate expires at the end of 1999.
The row over the Bank of France foreshadows another power struggle over the role of the future European Central Bank.
France has already said it wants ECB power on monetary policy to be offset by political control of exchange rates. It also wants policies to drive the dollar up against the euro.

And it wants a political decision on who will be the first head of the ECB, rather than going along with an assumption that the job would go, by mutual consent, to the orthodox head of the Dutch central bank, Wim Duisenberg.
Chirac's decision on the Bank of France council could be the first real test of his commitment to currency credibility.
